error_modes.label: Final approach airspeed control after FAF

texts.0: SP, due to a power setting selected without reference to the computed final approach airspeed, did not stabilize speed after the FAF and made no corrective throttle input as the trend developed. Airspeed diverged past plus 15 and minus 10 knots from the computed value and continued to drift while the descent was flown. IP had to direct the power change to recover the approach speed before the MAP.
texts.1: SP, due to a late and coarse throttle response to a decaying descent profile, did not hold the computed final approach airspeed after the FAF. Airspeed reached the plus 15 and minus 10 knot limit and was returned toward the computed value only after verbal prompting from IP. The correction was applied with a delay that left the speed unsettled into the MDA segment.
texts.2: SP, due to a power reduction made before the descent rate was established, allowed the computed final approach airspeed to erode after the FAF. Airspeed reached the band between plus 10 and plus 15 knots fast and minus 5 and minus 10 knots slow, but SP recognized the trend on the airspeed indicator and restored the computed value with a timely throttle correction and no intervention.
texts.3: SP set power against the computed final approach airspeed immediately after the FAF and held it through the descent to MDA. Airspeed stayed inside plus 10 and minus 5 knots of the computed value, with small anticipatory throttle corrections applied as configuration and descent rate changed. Speed control did not degrade course or altitude tracking.
texts.4: SP established the computed final approach airspeed at the FAF on the first power setting and flew the entire final segment with negligible speed excursions. Throttle inputs were small, anticipatory and matched to configuration and wind changes, so the airspeed indicator remained essentially steady from FAF to MAP. Speed discipline left full attention available for course and altitude control.
texts.marginal: SP kept the computed final approach airspeed within standards but worked the throttle in repeated large corrections, so speed oscillated close to the fast side of tolerance through the final segment. The trend was toward late recognition of the decaying descent profile rather than anticipation of it. SP is expected to set power against the computed airspeed at the FAF and refine it with small inputs on subsequent approaches.

texts_at.1: SP set power against the computed final approach airspeed to the standard expected at this stage, letting airspeed reach the plus 15 and minus 10 knot limit before it was returned toward the computed value. The return followed verbal prompting from the IP rather than SP's own throttle response to the decaying profile. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to respond to the descent profile with the throttle promptly rather than letting the profile decay before power is added.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the trend on the airspeed indicator without intervention, letting airspeed reach the band between plus 10 and 15 knots fast before a timely throttle correction restored the computed value. The power reduction is still made before the descent rate is established rather than with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set power together with the descent rate rather than reducing it before the rate is settled.
texts_at.3: SP set power against the computed final approach airspeed immediately after the FAF and held it through the descent to MDA on most of the segment, staying inside plus 10 and minus 5 knots of the computed value with small anticipatory throttle corrections. One correction was a little larger than the rest, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep that correction as small as the rest of the segment.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the trend on the airspeed indicator without intervention, letting airspeed reach the band between plus 10 and 15 knots fast before a timely throttle correction restored the computed value. Setting power together with the descent rate, rather than reducing it before the rate is settled, would keep that trend smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good throttle timing.
texts_above.3: SP set power against the computed final approach airspeed immediately after the FAF and held it through the descent to MDA, staying inside plus 10 and minus 5 knots of the computed value with small anticipatory throttle corrections that did not degrade course or altitude tracking. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good speed discipline.
texts_above.4: SP established the computed final approach airspeed at the FAF on the first power setting and flew the entire final segment with negligible speed excursions, throttle inputs small, anticipatory and matched to configuration and wind changes. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent throttle anticipation.

texts.0: SP, due to chasing raw course deviation with uncoordinated heading changes instead of establishing and holding a wind correction angle, did not maintain the published final approach course. Course displacement exceeded 8 degrees from the inbound radial and continued to increase toward the MAP. IP had to take corrective action to return the aircraft to the published course.
texts.1: SP, due to an unrecognized crosswind on the inbound radial, did not apply a wind correction angle and allowed the aircraft to drift steadily off the published course. Displacement reached the 8 degree limit and was corrected only after verbal instruction from IP, with the aircraft still recentering as MDA was approached. The correction was applied late and required more than one heading change to settle.
texts.2: SP, due to an initially insufficient wind correction angle after course intercept, allowed displacement from the inbound radial to grow into the band between 5 and 8 degrees. SP recognized the deviation on the course indicator, applied a measured heading correction, and reestablished the published course before the MDA segment without intervention.
texts.3: SP intercepted the published final approach course and held it inside 5 degrees throughout the inbound segment. A wind correction angle was established early and adjusted in small increments, so course deviation stayed centered rather than oscillating. Tracking was maintained through the descent without degrading airspeed or altitude control.
texts.4: SP intercepted the inbound radial cleanly and held the published course with negligible displacement to the MAP. The wind correction angle was identified within the first part of the final segment and required only minor refinement thereafter, keeping the course indicator effectively centered. Tracking precision was maintained while airspeed and altitude were simultaneously flown to tolerance.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the published final approach course within standards but tracked it with a repeating series of small overshoots either side of the radial rather than a settled wind correction angle. The trend was toward correcting deviation after it appeared instead of holding a computed drift correction. SP is expected to establish the wind correction angle at intercept and hold heading to keep the course indicator centered.

texts_at.1: SP tracked the published course to the standard expected at this stage, letting displacement reach the 8 degree limit before it was corrected. The correction followed verbal instruction from the IP rather than SP's own recognition of the crosswind. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to establish a wind correction angle at intercept rather than chasing raw course deviation with heading changes.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the deviation on the course indicator without intervention, letting displacement grow into the band between 5 and 8 degrees before a measured heading correction re-established the published course. The wind correction angle is still insufficient at course intercept before it is refined. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the wind correction angle correctly at intercept rather than refining an insufficient one afterward.
texts_at.3: SP intercepted the published final approach course and held it inside 5 degrees throughout the inbound segment on most of it, with a wind correction angle established early and adjusted in small increments so course deviation stayed centered rather than oscillating. One segment needed a slightly larger adjustment, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep that segment as centered as the rest of the approach.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the deviation on the course indicator without intervention, letting displacement grow into the band between 5 and 8 degrees before a measured heading correction re-established the published course. Sizing the wind correction angle correctly at intercept, rather than refining an insufficient one afterward, would keep that growth smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound course-tracking technique.
texts_above.3: SP intercepted the published final approach course and held it inside 5 degrees throughout the inbound segment, with a wind correction angle established early and adjusted in small increments so course deviation stayed centered rather than oscillating, tracking maintained through the descent without degrading airspeed or altitude control. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed drift correction.
texts_above.4: SP intercepted the inbound radial cleanly and held the published course with negligible displacement to the MAP, the wind correction angle identified within the first part of the final segment and requiring only minor refinement thereafter. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional tracking precision.

texts.0: SP, due to an unarrested descent rate approaching the published minimum descent altitude, did not level off at MDA and did not respect the zero tolerance below it. The aircraft went below MDA, or remained more than 200 feet above it while the MAP passed, without corrective action by SP. IP had to intervene on the controls to restore the published minimum descent altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power addition during the level off, did not capture the published minimum descent altitude at the planned point. Altitude settled at the 200 foot limit above MDA and was corrected toward the published value only after verbal prompting from IP. The delay consumed a significant part of the segment available before the MAP.
texts.2: SP, due to a descent rate not reduced early enough before level off, overshot the level altitude and stabilized between 100 and 200 feet above the published MDA. SP recognized the deviation on the altimeter, corrected with a timely descent to the published minimum descent altitude, and at no point descended below it or required intervention.
texts.3: SP anticipated the level off, reduced descent rate in time and captured the published minimum descent altitude within 100 feet above it with no descent below MDA. Altitude was then held steady to the MAP while course and airspeed were maintained. Power and pitch were coordinated so the level off did not disturb the approach speed.
texts.4: SP levelled off precisely at the published minimum descent altitude with negligible overshoot and no descent below it. Altitude was held essentially constant from level off to the MAP, with pitch and power coordinated so airspeed and course were unaffected by the transition. Altimeter control required no visible correction during the level segment.
texts.marginal: SP held the published minimum descent altitude within standards but captured it with a shallow oscillation and stayed consistently toward the upper part of the allowed band. The trend was toward starting the level off late and recovering the altitude rather than arriving at MDA already stabilized. SP is expected to anticipate the level off point and settle on the published minimum descent altitude with a single correction.

texts_at.1: SP captured the published minimum descent altitude to the standard expected at this stage, settling at the 200 foot limit above MDA before it was corrected toward the published value. The correction followed verbal prompting from the IP rather than SP's own reduction of the descent rate. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce descent rate early enough that the level-off happens without needing a verbal prompt to complete it.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the deviation on the altimeter without intervention, stabilizing between 100 and 200 feet above the published MDA before a timely descent corrected to the published minimum descent altitude. Descent rate is still reduced too late before the level off overshoots. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce descent rate earlier before level off so the aircraft is not corrected down to MDA after an overshoot.
texts_at.3: SP anticipated the level off, reduced descent rate in time and captured the published minimum descent altitude within 100 feet above it with no descent below MDA on most approaches, holding altitude steady to the MAP while course and airspeed were maintained. One approach needed a slightly later reduction than the rest, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to reduce that approach's rate as early as on the rest.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the deviation on the altimeter without intervention, stabilizing between 100 and 200 feet above the published MDA before a timely descent corrected to the published minimum descent altitude. Reducing descent rate earlier before level off, rather than after an overshoot, would keep that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady rate management.
texts_above.3: SP anticipated the level off, reduced descent rate in time and captured the published minimum descent altitude within 100 feet above it with no descent below MDA, holding altitude steady to the MAP while course and airspeed were maintained and power and pitch coordinated so the level off did not disturb approach speed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good level-off anticipation.
texts_above.4: SP levelled off precisely at the published minimum descent altitude with negligible overshoot and no descent below it, holding altitude essentially constant from level off to the MAP with pitch and power coordinated so airspeed and course were unaffected. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior altitude capture.

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete listening watch while setting up the approach, did not comply with an ATC instruction affecting the approach clearance. The assigned heading, altitude or clearance limit was not flown as issued and no readback was made that would have exposed the discrepancy, with the course displacement passing 8 degrees before it was noticed. IP had to intervene with ATC and on the controls to restore compliance.
texts.1: SP, due to a transmission received while the navigation aid was being retuned, did not act on an ATC instruction until the deviation was already established. Compliance was achieved only after IP prompted verbally, and the aircraft was at the edge of the cleared parameter, with the course displacement reaching 8 degrees, when the correction started. Readback was incomplete and did not include the assigned altitude.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed readback of an ATC instruction issued during the intercept, was late in starting the assigned turn or altitude change. SP detected the omission without prompting, read back the clearance correctly and complied within the approach parameters, with the course displacement staying near 6 degrees, so the deviation remained bounded and self-corrected.
texts.3: SP maintained an accurate listening watch throughout the approach, read back ATC instructions correctly and complied with each clearance promptly. Assigned headings, altitudes and clearance limits were flown as issued while the approach parameters were maintained. Radio work did not interrupt aircraft control or approach setup.
texts.4: SP handled all ATC instructions on the approach with correct, concise readbacks and immediate compliance, without any prompting. Clearances were integrated into the approach plan as they were received, so no assigned parameter was ever in question. Radio discipline was maintained with no measurable effect on flight parameter control.
texts.marginal: SP complied with all ATC instructions but consistently needed a repeat of the clearance before reading it back, and compliance began later than the traffic situation warranted. The trend was toward processing the instruction after the flying task rather than integrating the two. SP is expected to maintain a continuous listening watch and read back clearances on first transmission.

texts_at.1: SP complied with ATC instructions affecting the approach clearance to the standard expected at this stage, with the course displacement reaching 8 degrees before compliance was achieved. Compliance followed IP prompting verbally rather than SP's own listening watch. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to maintain a continuous listening watch while setting up the approach rather than missing an instruction because the navigation aid was being retuned.
texts_at.2: SP detected the omission without prompting, letting the course displacement stay near 6 degrees before reading back the clearance correctly and complying within the approach parameters. The readback is still delayed relative to the instruction being issued during the intercept. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to read back an instruction as it is issued during the intercept rather than after a delay.
texts_at.3: SP maintained an accurate listening watch throughout the approach, read back ATC instructions correctly and complied with each clearance promptly on most of the approach, with assigned headings, altitudes and clearance limits flown as issued. One instruction needed a brief follow-up, without a deviation resulting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to handle that instruction as cleanly as the rest of the approach.

texts_above.2: SP detected the omission without prompting, letting the course displacement stay near 6 degrees before reading back the clearance correctly and complying within the approach parameters. Reading back an instruction as it is issued, rather than after a delay, would keep that displacement smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent readback timing.
texts_above.3: SP maintained an accurate listening watch throughout the approach, read back ATC instructions correctly and complied with each clearance promptly, with assigned headings, altitudes and clearance limits flown as issued while approach parameters were maintained. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined radio management.
texts_above.4: SP handled all ATC instructions on the approach with correct, concise readbacks and immediate compliance without any prompting, clearances integrated into the approach plan as they were received. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless clearance integration.

texts.0: SP, due to reading the approach plate without cross-checking the step-down fixes against DME or radial position, violated a published routing or altitude restriction as depicted in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manuals. The aircraft descended below a published minimum segment altitude, or flew more than 8 degrees outside the depicted track. IP had to intervene to restore the published profile.
texts.1: SP, due to an unverified fix identification during the intermediate segment, initiated descent before the applicable step-down fix and crossed it about 200 ft above the published minimum, at the limit of tolerance. The profile was corrected only after IP pointed out the restriction, and the aircraft remained low on profile for part of the segment. The published routing itself was maintained.
texts.2: SP, due to a descent started slightly early against the depicted step-down profile, allowed the aircraft to approach the published segment minimum before the fix, crossing it about 150 ft above the published value, between the tolerances. SP cross-checked DME and the approach plate, recognized the discrepancy and arrested the descent in time, so no published routing or altitude restriction was violated and no intervention was required.
texts.3: SP flew the depicted routing and honored every published altitude restriction from the initial segment to the MAP. Step-down fixes were identified by DME or radial before descent was initiated, and segment minima were respected throughout. The approach plate was used actively rather than from memory.
texts.4: SP flew the published routing and every segment altitude restriction with negligible deviation and no reference error. Each step-down fix was positively identified before descent, and the resulting profile matched the depicted procedure throughout. Plate management was orderly enough that no restriction required a late check.
texts.marginal: SP respected all published routing and altitude restrictions but identified several step-down fixes only just before the descent point, leaving no margin for a misread. The trend was toward late confirmation of the depicted profile rather than early planning of it. SP is expected to brief and confirm the step-down fixes before the segment begins.

texts_at.1: SP honored the published routing and altitude restrictions to the standard expected at this stage, crossing the step-down fix about 200 ft above the published minimum, at the limit of tolerance, before the profile was corrected. The correction followed IP pointing out the restriction rather than SP's own fix identification. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to verify each fix identification during the intermediate segment before initiating the descent past it.
texts_at.2: SP cross-checked DME and the approach plate and arrested the descent in time without intervention, crossing the fix about 150 ft above the published value, between the tolerances. The descent is still started a little early against the depicted step-down profile before the cross-check catches it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to time the descent to the depicted step-down profile rather than starting it slightly early and correcting afterward.
texts_at.3: SP flew the depicted routing and honored every published altitude restriction from the initial segment to the MAP on most of the approach, with step-down fixes identified by DME or radial before descent was initiated. One fix was identified a little later than the rest, without a restriction being violated. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to identify that fix as early as the rest of the approach.

texts_above.2: SP cross-checked DME and the approach plate and arrested the descent in time without intervention, crossing the fix about 150 ft above the published value. Timing the descent to the depicted step-down profile, rather than starting it slightly early, would keep that margin steadier. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable profile timing.
texts_above.3: SP flew the depicted routing and honored every published altitude restriction from the initial segment to the MAP, with step-down fixes identified by DME or radial before descent was initiated and the approach plate used actively rather than from memory. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good plate management.
texts_above.4: SP flew the published routing and every segment altitude restriction with negligible deviation and no reference error, each step-down fix positively identified before descent so the resulting profile matched the depicted procedure throughout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior routing accuracy.

error_modes.label: Approach setup, navaid tuning and identification

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate workload management during the approach phase, did not complete the approach setup before the intercept and did not tune and identify the VOR or TACAN facility for the final approach course. The approach was flown on an unverified or incorrect navigation source, contrary to the standardized procedures of AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the Flight Manual, with the course displacement exceeding 8 degrees on the intercept. IP had to intervene to correct the navigation setup.
texts.1: SP, due to task sequencing that left the approach setup until after the descent had begun, did not tune, identify and set the final approach course in time for a stabilized intercept. The setup was completed only after IP prompted, and the intercept was flown at 8 degrees, the outer limit of the course tolerance, while the equipment was still being configured. No item was left unset at the FAF.
texts.2: SP, due to a compressed task sequence on the transition to the approach, was late in identifying the VOR or TACAN facility and in setting the final approach course, with the course displacement reaching about 6 degrees, between the desired and the maximum tolerance. SP detected the omission during the approach check, completed the setup before the intercept without prompting, and the approach was flown on a verified navigation source throughout.
texts.3: SP completed the approach setup in good time, tuned and positively identified the VOR or TACAN facility and set the final approach course before the intercept. The sequence followed the standardized procedures of AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the Flight Manual with no omitted item. Setup work was spread so that aircraft control was never interrupted.
texts.4: SP planned and executed the approach setup ahead of the aircraft, with the facility tuned and identified and all navigation and cockpit items configured well before the intercept. The sequence matched the standardized procedures exactly and left spare capacity for the ATC and flying tasks. No setup item required rework at any stage of the approach.
texts.marginal: SP completed the full approach setup and identified the facility correctly, but the work was compressed into the last part of the transition and left little margin before the intercept. The trend was toward reactive rather than planned task sequencing under increasing approach workload. SP is expected to complete the tune, identify and course set earlier so the intercept is flown from a settled cockpit.

texts_at.1: SP completed the approach setup to the standard expected at this stage, flying the intercept at 8 degrees, the outer limit of the course tolerance, while the equipment was still being configured. The setup followed IP prompting rather than SP's own task sequencing. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to sequence the approach setup before the descent begins rather than leaving it until after the descent has started.
texts_at.2: SP detected the omission during the approach check without prompting, letting the course displacement reach about 6 degrees, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before completing the setup before the intercept. The task sequence on the transition to the approach is still compressed before the omission is caught. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to spread the transition tasks earlier so the sequence is not compressed at the transition itself.
texts_at.3: SP completed the approach setup in good time, tuned and positively identified the VOR or TACAN facility and set the final approach course before the intercept on most of the approach, following the standardized procedures with no omitted item. One item was completed a little later than the rest, without a deviation resulting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to complete that item as promptly as the rest of the setup.

texts_above.2: SP detected the omission during the approach check without prompting, letting the course displacement reach about 6 degrees before completing the setup before the intercept. Spreading the transition tasks earlier, rather than compressing them at the transition, would keep that displacement smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid task sequencing.
texts_above.3: SP completed the approach setup in good time, tuned and positively identified the VOR or TACAN facility and set the final approach course before the intercept, following the standardized procedures of AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the Flight Manual with no omitted item and aircraft control never interrupted. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate setup timing.
texts_above.4: SP planned and executed the approach setup ahead of the aircraft, with the facility tuned and identified and all navigation and cockpit items configured well before the intercept, leaving spare capacity for the ATC and flying tasks. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary setup planning.

texts.0: SP, due to an unmonitored station passage or DME reference, did not execute the required actions at the FAF and did not initiate the descent at the correct point. Time, configuration or descent initiation were wrong to the extent that the profile could not reach MDA before the MAP without an excessive descent rate, with the aircraft still more than 200 ft above the published minimum descent altitude approaching the MAP. IP had to intervene to reestablish the published descent profile.
texts.1: SP, due to an ambiguous station passage indication that was not cross-checked against DME, delayed the FAF actions and started the descent late. Descent initiation was at the limit of what the segment allowed, and the required rate had to be increased after IP prompted the correction, with the aircraft 200 ft above MDA, at the tolerance limit, when the correction began. Timing and configuration items at the FAF were completed out of the standard sequence.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on course centering at station passage, was late by a short interval in starting time and initiating the descent at the FAF. SP recognized the omission promptly, completed the FAF actions and adjusted descent rate within normal limits, crossing MDA with about 150 ft of margin, between the tolerances, so that MDA was reached in good time without intervention.
texts.3: SP identified the FAF positively, started time where required and initiated the descent at the correct point with the aircraft correctly configured. The descent rate selected was appropriate to groundspeed and the remaining distance to MDA. FAF actions were executed in the standardized sequence without omission.
texts.4: SP executed the FAF sequence precisely at station passage, with time started, configuration set and descent initiated in one coordinated flow. The descent rate was computed to groundspeed so that MDA was reached with an unhurried margin before the MAP. No FAF item was late or repeated.
texts.marginal: SP completed all FAF actions and started the descent within standards, but the sequence was executed item by item after station passage rather than as a prepared flow, leaving the descent slightly late. The trend was toward reacting to the fix instead of anticipating it. SP is expected to have the FAF actions prepared and to initiate the descent immediately at station passage.

texts_at.1: SP executed the FAF actions to the standard expected at this stage, remaining 200 ft above MDA, at the tolerance limit, when the correction began. The correction followed IP prompting rather than SP's own cross-check of station passage against DME. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to cross-check an ambiguous station passage indication against DME rather than delaying the FAF actions until it resolves itself.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the omission promptly and completed the FAF actions without intervention, crossing MDA with about 150 ft of margin, between the tolerances, so MDA was reached in good time. Attention is still held on course centering at the moment of station passage before the FAF actions are started. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to divide attention between course centering and the FAF actions at station passage rather than one after the other.
texts_at.3: SP identified the FAF positively, started time where required and initiated the descent at the correct point with the aircraft correctly configured on most approaches, the descent rate selected appropriate to groundspeed and the remaining distance to MDA. One approach needed a slightly later rate selection, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to select that rate as promptly as on the rest of the approaches.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the omission promptly and completed the FAF actions without intervention, crossing MDA with about 150 ft of margin, so MDA was reached in good time. Dividing attention between course centering and the FAF actions at station passage, rather than one after the other, would keep that margin tighter. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured task division.
texts_above.3: SP identified the FAF positively, started time where required and initiated the descent at the correct point with the aircraft correctly configured, the descent rate selected appropriate to groundspeed and the remaining distance to MDA with FAF actions executed in the standardized sequence without omission. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise FAF execution.
texts_above.4: SP executed the FAF sequence precisely at station passage, with time started, configuration set and descent initiated in one coordinated flow, the descent rate computed to groundspeed so MDA was reached with an unhurried margin before the MAP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate sequence coordination.

error_modes.label: Instrument cross-check during the final segment

texts.0: SP, due to a scan that fixated on the course indicator to the exclusion of the other instruments, did not cross-check attitude, altitude and airspeed during the final segment. Deviations in the unmonitored parameters developed unnoticed and were still increasing when they exceeded approach tolerances, with airspeed drifting more than 15 knots fast before the scan caught it. IP had to intervene to reestablish the flight parameters.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan narrowed onto the parameter being corrected, did not cross-check the remaining instruments and let a second parameter drift to the limit of tolerance while the first was being fixed, with airspeed reaching 15 knots fast, at the limit, before recovery began. The drift was recognized only after IP called it out, and recovery of both parameters was still in progress at MDA. The scan remained sequential rather than integrated for the rest of the segment.
texts.2: SP, due to an interrupted cross-check while retuning and rechecking the navigation display, allowed a secondary parameter to move into the outer part of the approach tolerance band, with airspeed reaching about 12 knots fast. SP restored a full instrument scan without prompting, detected the deviation on the next sweep and corrected it in time, keeping all parameters within limits.
texts.3: SP maintained a continuous cross-check of attitude, course, altitude and airspeed throughout the final segment. Deviations were detected while still small and corrected with single measured inputs, so no parameter approached its tolerance. The scan absorbed the radio and configuration tasks without breaking.
texts.4: SP flew the final segment on a fully integrated instrument cross-check, detecting trends before they became deviations. All approach parameters were held with negligible excursion while ATC calls and cockpit tasks were handled in stride. The scan rate never narrowed onto a single instrument, even during the level off at MDA.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the approach parameters within standards but the cross-check visibly slowed each time a correction was made, so the other instruments were sampled less often during those periods. The trend was toward a scan that narrows under a single-parameter correction. SP is expected to keep the full cross-check running while correcting, so trends are detected before deviations develop.

texts_at.1: SP cross-checked the instruments to the standard expected at this stage, letting airspeed reach 15 knots fast, at the limit, before recovery began. The recovery followed IP calling out the drift rather than SP's own broadened scan. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to cross-check the remaining instruments while a parameter is being corrected rather than narrowing the scan onto it alone.
texts_at.2: SP restored a full instrument scan without prompting, letting airspeed reach about 12 knots fast before the deviation was detected on the next sweep and corrected in time. The cross-check is still interrupted while retuning and rechecking the navigation display before it is restored. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the cross-check running through a navigation retune rather than interrupting it for that task.
texts_at.3: SP maintained a continuous cross-check of attitude, course, altitude and airspeed throughout the final segment on most of it, deviations detected while still small and corrected with single measured inputs so no parameter approached its tolerance. One interval showed a slightly longer pause between checks, without a deviation developing. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep that interval as short as the rest of the segment.

texts_above.2: SP restored a full instrument scan without prompting, letting airspeed reach about 12 knots fast before the deviation was detected on the next sweep and corrected in time. Keeping the cross-check running through a navigation retune, rather than interrupting it, would keep that drift smaller. texts.marginal: SP applied an airspeed increase for the gusty conditions but sized it to the steady wind rather than to the gust spread, so the margin was thin on the strongest gusts. Airspeed stayed within the code 3 tolerance, dipping close to 5 knots below the computed value twice, with the trend worsening as the aircraft descended toward the MDA. SP is expected to base the correction on the gust factor and adjust the flap setting to match.

texts_at.1: SP corrected for gusty conditions to the standard expected at this stage, letting excursions reach about 10 knots slow and 15 knots fast, at the code 1 limits, before they were contained. Containment followed IP directing a gust correction and a fixed torque setting rather than SP's own airspeed increase for the reported gusts. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to increase approach airspeed for the reported gust factor rather than flying gusty conditions at the plain computed speed.
texts_at.2: SP recognised the conditions required a higher speed and adjusted it without prompting, letting airspeed drop roughly 7 knots below the computed value in one gust, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, before the remainder of the approach was held steady. The airspeed increase is still added only after the FAF rather than before it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to add the airspeed increase before the FAF rather than after recognising the gusty conditions late.
texts_at.3: SP configured with the appropriate flap setting and increased the approach airspeed for the reported crosswind and gusts before the FAF on most of the approach, airspeed staying within the code 3 tolerance despite the gusts. One gust needed a slightly larger correction, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold that correction to the same margin as the rest of the approach.

texts_above.2: SP recognised the conditions required a higher speed and adjusted it without prompting, letting airspeed drop roughly 7 knots below the computed value in one gust before the remainder of the approach was held steady. Adding the airspeed increase before the FAF, rather than after recognising the gusts late, would keep that dip smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good gust-correction timing.
texts_above.3: SP configured with the appropriate flap setting and increased the approach airspeed for the reported crosswind and gusts before the FAF, airspeed staying within the code 3 tolerance of the computed value despite the gusts. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good gust management.
texts_above.4: SP briefed the gust factor, configured accordingly and flew a gust corrected approach airspeed held with small torque adjustments, excursions from the corrected value staying within about 3 knots through the whole final segment. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent gust anticipation.
